Pursuant to the authority vested in the Governor of the State of Colorado and, in particular,
pursuant to relevant portions of the Colorado Disaster Emergency Act, C.R.S. § 24-33.5-701, et
seq., I, John W. Hickenlooper, Governor of the State of Colorado, hereby issue this Executive
Order reauthorizing and amending Executive Order D 2013-017 declaring a disaster emergency
due to the West Fork Fire Complex in Mineral, Rio Grande, and Hinsdale Counties, Colorado.
Background and Purpose
The Governor is responsible for meeting the dangers to the state and people presented by
disasters. C.R.S. § 24-33.5-704(1). The Colorado Disaster Emergency Act defines a disaster as
"the occurrence or imminent threat of widespread or severe damages, injury or loss of life or
property resulting from any natural cause or cause of human origin, including but not limited to
fire, flood [and] water contamination ...." C.R.S. § 24-33.5-703(3).
On June 5, 2013, lightning started the West Fork Fire in the San Juan National Forest in Mineral
County. By June 21, 2013, the West Fork Fire Complex had grown to over 29,000 acres and the
Governor verbally declared a disaster emergency. By July 23, 2013, the West Fork Complex Fire
had grown to 109,615 acres and was 66% contained. The fire continues to burn inside its
perimeter and the large amount of beetle kill trees and forecasted hot and dry weather
exacerbate the likelihood of continued extreme fire behavior.
Emergency medical providers from outside Colorado continue to support firefighters on the
West Fork Fire Complex and other large wildfires in Colorado, especially in northwest Colorado.
In non-emergency circumstances, an individual providing emergency medical services in
Colorado must possess a certification issued by the Colorado Department of Public Health and
Environment. C.R.S. § 25-3.5-203(1)(b). During a disaster emergency, the Governor is
---PAGE---
Executive Order D 2013-022
July 25, 2013
Page 2 of 4
authorized to suspend the provisions of any regulatory statute or the regulations of any state
agency if strict compliance with the provisions of the statute or regulation would in any way
"prevent, hinder, or delay necessary action in coping with the emergency." C.R.S. § 24-33.5-
704(7)(a).
The West Fork Complex Fire severely damaged critical watersheds and forest soils, resulting in
threats to water supplies and increasing the likelihood of severe flooding. Rainfall runoff in
wildfire burn areas is significantly increased from pre-fire conditions due to loss of vegetation
and changed soil conditions. As a result, lands within and downstream of burn areas will
experience an increased threat of flooding for a number of years after the fire. Until burned
watersheds recover, effective flood damage reduction tools include local preparedness, risk
awareness, flood insurance policies, and mitigation. Further, the West Fork Fire Complex is
located in an area of the state known to experience gaps in available weather radar due to
terrain blockage of radar beams.
These conditions create an immediate need for financial relief in the West Fork Fire Complex
burn area. Installations of weather radar infrastructure (either temporary or permanent),
along with rain gauges and stream gauges at key locations, are needed to help develop a fully
functioning flood alert system for the endangered watersheds and communities.
However, federal funds that normally help in post-fire flood mitigation and watershed
management have been impaired due to federal sequestration. In light of these exceptional
circumstances, on July 17, 2013, the Colorado Water Conservation Board unanimously elected
to release $2,500,000 from the Colorado Water Conservation Board's Severance Tax Trust Fund
Perpetual Base Account to Hinsdale County to help in post-fire mitigation, emergency
preparedness and flood mitigation - including rain gauges and radar equipment to provide
early warnings for flooding.
This Executive Order reauthorizes the state of disaster emergency for the West Fork Fire
Complex, and orders that $2,500,000 from the Colorado Water Conservation Board's Severance
Tax Trust Fund Perpetual Base Account be utilized to help protect communities and natural
resources in the West Fork Fire Complex burn area from post-wildfire dangers.
---PAGE---

July 25, 2013
Page 3 of 4
Il.

A. The West Fork Fire Complex continues to constitute a disaster emergency for purposes
of C.R.S. § 24-33.5-701, et seq.
B. Due to the extent of the West Fork Fire Complex and other wildfires burning in
Colorado, C.R.S. § 25-3.5-203(1)(b) is suspended for providers directly in support of wildfire
suppression operations who hold current emergency medical services provider licensure or

or any state or territory in the United States until this Executive Order expires. C.R.S. § 24-
33.5-704(7)(a).

its designated representative, shall formally present this report to the Colorado Water
Conservation Board no later than 120 days after completion of the relief efforts.

Background and Purpose
The Governor is responsible for meeting the dangers to the state and people presented
by disasters. The Colorado Disaster Emergency Act defines a disaster as "the occurrence or
imminent threat of widespread or severe damages, injury or loss of life or property resulting
from any natural cause or cause of human origin, including but not limited to ... flood." C.R.S.
924-33.5-703(3).
During the period of August 1, 2013, to August 15, 2013, and continuing, the annual rainy
"monsoon" season in Colorado produced numerous thunderstorms resulting in rainfall rates of
up to 2" per hour. Unfortunately, this weather phenomenon follows three years of severe
drought and two years of record loss wildfire seasons. Wildfire burn scars are at greater risk (3-
10 times) of flooding from rainfall. On August 9, 2013, thunderstorms produced up to 1.6 of
rainfall on the Waldo Canyon Fire burn scar. This resulted in severe flooding of multiple
canyons in the Waldo Canyon Fire burn scar. The flood waters, with accompanying mud, rock,
and debris, flowed on to U.S. Highway 24 and into Manitou Springs. The flooding killed one
person, and injured at least three others. In addition, the flood caused major damage to the
highway, property, and infrastructure in El Paso County in the vicinity of the Waldo Canyon Fire
---PAGE---

August 16, 2013
Page 2 of 3
burn scar, including the City of Manitou Springs. The flood event destroyed at least one
structure, damaged at least twenty additional structures, and destroyed the eastbound ramp
from U.S. Highway 24 to the City of Manitou Springs.
On August 10, 2013, El Paso County and the City of Manitou Springs requested state assistance
with debris removal and emergency protective measures. I approved this request and verbally
declared a disaster emergency for the flooding in El Paso County.

agencies shall take whatever actions may be required and requested by the Director of the

as necessary.

be insufficient to pay for the flood debris removal and emergency protective measures
efforts related to the El Paso County Flood. Therefore, it is ordered that $400,000 be
transferred into the Disaster Emergency Fund from the General Fund appropriation in Fiscal
Year 2013-14 to the Controlled Maintenance Trust Fund. It is further ordered that this
$400,000 from the Disaster Emergency Fund is encumbered to pay for the flood debris
removal and emergency protective measures efforts related to the El Paso County Flood.
The Director of the Office of Emergency Management is hereby authorized and directed to
allocate the funding to the appropriate government agencies and execute awards, purchase
orders or other mechanisms to effect the allocation of the funds. These funds shall remain
available for this purpose for eighteen months from the date of this Executive Order, and
any unexpended funds shall remain in the Disaster Emergency Fund.
D. The Colorado Department of Public Safety is authorized and directed to coordinate
application to the federal government for funds available for reimbursement and to
coordinate application for any other funds available related to this disaster emergency.

Executive Order, except that the funds described in paragraph II (C) above shall remain
available for the described purposes for eighteen months from the date of this Executive Order.

Beginning on September 11, 2013, heavy rainfall fell west of Interstate 25 from south of
Colorado Springs to the Wyoming border. The greatest impact was in Boulder County, where
up to eight inches of rain fell by 0700 hours on September 12, 2013. Rainfall continues with the
National Weather Service predicting another 2 - 4 inches by 0700 hours on September 13,
2013. While authorities cannot conduct damage assessments until the rainfall subsides and the
flooding recedes; known consequences are three fatalities, three injuries, damage to a natural
gas distribution pipeline, power outages, at least two structures destroyed, water damage to

the Town of Lyons wastewater treatment system.

verbally approved this request. At approximately 0235 hours, Boulder County upgraded the

Background and Purpose
The Governor is responsible for meeting the dangers to the state and people presented

imminent threat of widespread or severe damages, injury or loss of life or property resulting

On September 13, 2013, I issued Executive Order D 2013-26 declaring a Disaster Emergency in

additional rainfall. As of September 18, 2013, the National Weather Service reported that 7-day
rain totals have reached as high as 18.1 inches in Boulder County, 12.4 inches in Larimer
County, 15.6 inches in Adams County, and 11.6 inches in El Paso County. Initial estimates of the
casualties and property damage are as follows: six persons are deceased, 17,648 structures
have been damaged, which includes 4,047 structures that have been destroyed, 30 bridges
have been destroyed, and 20 others have been seriously damaged. As of 1100 on September

September 19, 2013
Page 2 of 4
18, 2013, a total of 754 troops, 19 helicopters, 20 ground search-and-rescue teams, and 67
traffic-control points were operational.
After the Executive Order was issued on September 13, 2013, I verbally declared a disaster
emergency and activated the State Emergency Operations Plan in two additional counties, Clear
Creek and Sedgwick, because of significant rainfall to that area.
In Executive Order D 2013-26, I ordered that $6,000,000 be transferred into the Disaster
Emergency Fund. The estimated cost of disaster relief so far has been approximately $ 3.5
million per day, and the Acting Director of the Office of Emergency Management estimates that
75% of the funds originally ordered had been expended as of September 16, 2013. As extensive
relief efforts continue, I find that the $6,000,000 that was originally ordered is insufficient to
pay for the flood response and recovery.
As a result of the recent flooding, Colorado's transportation infrastructure has been
significantly compromised, limiting the ability of the citizens of Colorado to access their homes,
businesses and farms and negatively impacting our ability to provide necessary goods and
services to the hardest hit counties. The severity of the damage to the transportation
infrastructure, taken together with the brevity of time before winter weather conditions set in,
requires extraordinary measures to assist in the reconstruction and repair of Colorado's
transportation infrastructure.
The flooding has also damaged businesses and hindered their ability to provide their
communities with essential goods and services including food and other daily necessities.
Extraordinary measures are necessary to reopen food service businesses promptly in a manner
that does not compromise food safety but also recognizes that the rules and regulations in
normal times might be unduly burdensome under the circumstances.
Il.

Pursuant to the authority vested in the Governor of the State of Colorado and, in
particular, pursuant to relevant portions of C.R.S. § 28-3-104 and relevant portions of the
Colorado Disaster Emergency Act, C.R.S. § 24-33.5-701, et seq., 1, John W. Hickenlooper,
Governor of the State of Colorado, hereby issue this Executive Order declaring a disaster
emergency due to the imminent winter storm.
Background and Purpose
The Governor is responsible for meeting the dangers to the State and people presented
by disasters. The Colorado Disaster Emergency Act defines a disaster as "the occurrence or
imminent threat of widespread or severe damages, injury or loss of life or property resulting
from any natural cause or cause of human origin, including but not limited to ... storm."
C.R.S. § 24-33.5-703(3).
The National Weather Service has issued winter storm warnings for multiple regions of
Colorado because of a cold upper level disturbance that has moved into the State. This storm
system is forecasted to remain over the region through Wednesday, December 4, and to drop
Fahrenheit temperatures into the single digits with overnight lows well below zero degrees.
Strong winds ahead of this weather system are predicted to impede visibility and make travel
difficult. Snow is expected to intensify from north to south across the mountains and spread
into the foothills and plains this afternoon and evening. The snow is anticipated to be
moderate to heavy, at times, especially in and around the mountains and foothills. With the
slow movement of the storm system, snow is expected to continue through much
of Wednesday, December 4, before gradually decreasing later that day.
Total snow accumulations are projected to be 1 to 3 feet for the mountains, 6 to 12 inches for
the western urban corridor, and 2 to 6 inches for the rest of the plains. Significant amounts of
---PAGE---
Executive Order D 2013-032
December 3, 2013
Page 2 of 2
snow are likely to make travel extremely dangerous, especially given the recent road damage
caused by the historic flooding in September. Due to the scope and duration of this imminent
winter storm and the need to respond quickly to any emergency situations, I verbally declared a
disaster emergency today at 1109 hours and activated the State Emergency Operations Plan.
Il.
Declaration and Directives
A. The imminent winter storm constitutes a disaster emergency under C.R.S.
§ 24-33.5-704. My verbal order of today, at 1109 hours, declaring a disaster emergency
is hereby memorialized by this Executive Order and shall have the full force and effect of
law as if it were contained within this Executive Order.
B. The State Emergency Operations Plan is hereby activated. All State departments and
agencies shall take whatever actions may be required and requested by the Director or
Acting Director of the Office of Emergency Management, including provision of
appropriate staff and equipment as necessary.
C. Pursuant to C.R.S. § 28-3-104, my verbal orders of today, at 1109 hours, activating the
National Guard and authorizing the utilization of National Guard assets for storm-
related missions is hereby memorialized by this Executive Order and shall have the full
force and effect of law as if it was contained within this Executive Order.
III.
Duration
This Executive Order shall expire thirty days from December 3, 2013, unless extended
further by Executive Order.
GIVEN under my hand and the
Executive Seal of the State of
Colorado this third day of
December, 2013.

Governor

EXECUTIVE ORDER
Declaring a State of Disaster Emergency Due to Extreme Winter Weather and
Authorizing a Temporary Exception to the Hours-of-Service Regulations for
Commercial Motor Vehicles Used in the Transportation of Propane
Pursuant to the authority vested in the Governor of the State of Colorado
and, in particular, pursuant to relevant portions of the Colorado Disaster Emergency
Act, C.R.S. § 24-33.5-700, et seq., and specifically C.R.S. § 24-33.5-704(7)(a), I, John
W. Hickenlooper, Governor of the State of Colorado, hereby issue this Executive
Order declaring a state of disaster emergency due to extreme weather conditions and
suspending the hours-of-service regulations in Colorado Revised Statutes § 42-4-235, to
the extent that the requirements therein prevent drivers of commercial motor vehicles
who are working on this emergency from transporting propane winter heating fuel.
Background and Purpose
Temperatures in Colorado have dropped below zero for consecutive weeks. The recent
extreme winter weather has caused an emergency situation by significantly reducing the
availability of propane and impeding the delivery of necessary propane to many areas of
Colorado. The extreme winter weather caused the cost of propane to skyrocket across
the country and significantly reduced the supply. The commercial vehicle industry is
impeded from continuing statewide propane fuel delivery operations for winter heating
purposes. As a result, many Coloradans are left without a mechanism to heat their
homes.
The Governor is responsible for meeting the dangers to the state and people presented
by disasters. The Colorado Disaster Emergency Act defines a disaster as "the occurrence
or imminent threat of widespread or severe damages, injury or loss of life or property
resulting from any natural cause or cause of human origin." C.R.S. § 24-33.5-703(3).
Colorado Revised Statutes § 42-4-235, adopting hours-of-service regulations from
49 C.F.R. 395, sets the hours which commercial vehicle drivers may operate. Those
restrictions are impeding the commercial vehicle industry from delivering fuel to
Coloradans in need.
---PAGE---
Executive Order D 2014-003
February 7, 2014
Page 2 of 2
Il.
Declaration and Directives
I declare and direct, as follows:
A. The provisions of C.R.S. § 42-4-235 are hereby suspended to the extent that they
prevent the delivery of necessary propane winter heating fuel to distribution
points within Colorado.
B. The above mentioned directive is subject to the following conditions:
i. This exception shall not be construed as an exemption from C.R.S. Title
42, Traffic Code, as it relates to general motor vehicle safety, state and
federal financial responsibility requirements, commercial driver's license
requirements, size and weight regulations, or any federal motor carrier
safety regulations not specifically identified herein.
ii. This exception shall also not be construed as an exemption from 49
CFR 392.4 which prohibits ill or fatigued drives from operating a motor
vehicle.
ili. Motor carriers or drivers currently subject to an out-of-state service
order issued by the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration are not
eligible for the exception until that order expires or the conditions have
been met.
Ill.
Duration
Unless amended or terminated by subsequent executive order, this order shall remain
in effect through March 7, 2014.
GIVEN under my hand and the
Executive Seal of the State of
Colorado this seventh day of
February, 2014

in the Wildfire Preparedness Fund for Wildfire Preparedness Activities
Pursuant to the authority vested in the Governor of the State of Colorado and, in
particular, pursuant to article IV, section 2 of the Colorado Constitution and section
24-33.5-1227(1)(b) of the Colorado Revised Statutes, I, John W. Hickenlooper, Governor of the
State of Colorado, hereby issue this Executive Order implementing the 2014 Wildfire
Preparedness Plan and designating moneys in the Wildfire Preparedness Fund for wildfire
preparedness activities.
1.
Background and Purpose
The Director ("Director") of the Division of Fire Prevention and Control ("Division") is
required to develop an annual Wildfire Preparedness Plan in collaboration with the County
Sheriffs of Colorado, the Colorado State Fire Chiefs' Association, the Director of the Office of
Emergency Management, and the Adjutant General. C.R.S. § 24-33.5-1227(2)(a).
The Wildfire Preparedness Plan shall be designed to address the following:
(1) The amount of aerial firefighting resources necessary for the State of Colorado at
times of high and low wildfire risk;
(2) The availability of appropriate aerial firefighting equipment and personnel at
times of high fire risk to respond to a wildfire;
(3) The availability of state wildfire engines and staffing of the engines at different
levels of wildfire risk;
(4) The availability of wildfire hand crews, including state inmate wildfire hand
crews, at different levels of wildfire risk; and
(5) A process for ordering and dispatching aerial firefighting equipment and
personnel that is consistent with, and supportive of, the statewide all-hazards
resource mobilization plan prepared pursuant to C.R.S. § 24-33.5-705.4.
---PAGE---
Executive Order D 2014-008
May 12, 2014
Page 2 of 3
The Wildfire Preparedness Plan shall also provide recommendations on the use of the
Wildfire Preparedness Fund created in C.R.S. § 24-33.5-1227(1)(a).
The Director prepared a draft of the Wildfire Preparedness Plan on March 27, 2014, which was
to be submitted to the Governor and the Members of the General Assembly in accordance with
C.R.S. § 24-33.5-1227(b). However, the draft could not be finalized because of uncertainty
about the fire aviation program. The Director submitted a finalized plan to the Advisory
Committee ("Advisory Committee") on Wildland Fire and Prescribed Fire Matters at its next
regularly scheduled meeting on April 24, 2014. The Advisory Committee adopted the plan, and
the Director submitted it to the Governor and Members of the General Assembly on April 28,
2014. The Wildfire Preparedness Plan reflects the collaboration of the County Sheriffs of
Colorado, the Colorado State Fire Chiefs' Association, the Director of the Office of Emergency
Management, and the Adjutant General.
Il.
Declaration and Directives
A. The Division is hereby directed to implement the Wildfire Preparedness Plan for
2014 and carry out the wildfire preparedness activities identified therein.
B. The Division shall use the moneys in the Wildfire Preparedness Fund to
implement and carry out the wildfire preparedness activities identified in the
2014 Wildfire Preparedness Plan, as is necessary.
III.
Duration
This Executive Order shall expire upon issuing an Executive Order or Proclamation
implementing the Wildfire Preparedness Plan for 2015, or upon rescission by subsequent
Executive Order.

EXECUTIVE ORDER
Rescinding Executive Order D 2012-006, Regarding Suspending Prescribed or
Controlled Fire Pending Review of Protocols
Pursuant to the authority vested in the Governor of the State of Colorado and, in
particular, pursuant to Article IV, section 2 of the Colorado Constitution, I, John W.
Hickenlooper, Governor of the State of Colorado, hereby issue this Executive Order rescinding
Executive Order D 2012-006.
Background and Purpose
On March 28, 2012, pursuant to Colorado Constitution, article IV, section 13 and C.R.S. 23-31-
308, we issued Executive Order D 2012-006 suspending prescribed or controlled fire on State or
private lands pending review of agency protocols for prescribed or controlled fire. The
suspension applied to all State lands as well as State agencies that applied prescribed or
controlled fire on non-State lands under contracts or agreements with other entities. At the
time, Colorado was experiencing unseasonably high temperatures and dry conditions which led
to a number of wildfires across the State, and one fire, the Lower North Fork Fire, had been
started by a prescribed or controlled burn.
On April 13, 2012, the Lower North Fork Prescribed Fire Review (Bass Report) was issued, which
made six recommendations for improving agency protocols around the use of prescribed burns.
On January 30, 2013, pursuant to Colorado Constitution, article IV, section 13 and C.R.S. 23-31-
308, we issued Executive Order D 2013-002, which amended Executive Order D 2012-006, to
allow for the resumption of slash pile burnings under controlled conditions in order to best
protect residents on the wildland-urban interface and promote the health and well being of our
forests. Broadcast burning however, remained banned pursuant to Executive Order D 2012-
006, pending a review of agency protocols.
---PAGE---
Executive Order D 2015-002
March 30, 2015
Page 2 of 3
On December 10, 2014, the Colorado Division of Fire Prevention and Control (Division) issued
its response to the Bass report recommendations. The response details the Division's
evaluation, assessment and implementation of procedures in response to each of the Bass
Report recommendations.
Wildfires threaten public health and safety and can cause catastrophic damage to public and
private resources, including clean air, clean water, fish and wildlife habitat, timber resources,
forest soils, scenic beauty, recreational opportunities, economic and employment
opportunities, and structures and other improvements.
Prescribed burning, which reduces naturally occurring vegetative fuels within a variety of
ecosystems, including forests and grasslands, reduces the risk and severity of major wildfire,
thereby lessening the threat of fire and the resulting loss of life and property in those areas,
including:
A. When applied to forest lands, prescribed burning serves to reduce hazardous
accumulations of fuels, prepare sites for both natural and artificial forest
regeneration, improve wildlife habitat, control insects and disease, and perpetuate
fire-dependent ecosystems; and
B. When prescribed burning is used to manage fuels in wildland-urban interface areas,
it substantially reduces the threat of damaging wildfire in urban communities.
The Division has developed new guidelines and procedures for prescribed burning to ensure
that all such burns are conducted in a safe and effective manner. These guidelines and
procedures represent best practices for prescribed burning and have been subjected to peer
evaluation and public comment.
II. Declaration and Directives
A. Executive Order D 2012-006 (Suspending Prescribed or Controlled Fire Pending
Review of Protocols) is hereby rescinded to allow for the resumption of prescribed
burning on State lands or by State agencies under controlled conditions.
B. Prescribed fire operations conducted by State agencies or on State lands shall
comply with the requirements of the Colorado Prescribed Burning Act (Senate Bill
13-083, as codified in C.R.S. Section 24-33.5-1201, et seq.) and the rules and
guidelines promulgated by the Division, to ensure that all such burns are conducted
in a safe and effective manner.
---PAGE---
Executive Order D 2015-002
March 30, 2015
Page 3 of 3
C. State agencies conducting prescribed burns shall observe the following additional
guidelines for prescribed burning:
1. Prescribed burning shall occur only after a determination has been made that
the property owner or other person having legal control of the property has both
evaluated all alternatives to prescribed burning and concluded that prescribed
burning is an appropriate hazardous fuel reduction method for the property; and
2. Prescribed burning shall occur only after proper notification of residents of
potentially affected areas, local government officials, and the Division.
D. The Division will work to ensure continued safety and protection for residents on the
wildland-urban interface, while promoting the health and longevity of our State's
natural forests through properly regulated prescribed burning.
III.
Duration
This Executive Order shall remain in effect until rescinded or modified by Executive Order.
GIVEN under my hand and the
Executive Seal of the State of
Colorado this thirtieth day of
March, 2015.

ohn W. Hickenloope
Governor

Declaring a Disaster Emergency and Authorizing National Guard Assets
in Response to Severe Weather, Associated Flooding, and a Landslide on State Highway 13
Pursuant to the authority vested in the Governor of the State of Colorado and,
in particular, pursuant relevant portions of C.R.S. § 28-3-104 and relevant portions of the
Colorado Disaster Emergency Act, C.R.S. § 24-33.5-701, et seq., 1, Joseph A. Garcia,
Lieutenant Governor of the State of Colorado, hereby issue this Executive Order
declaring a state disaster emergency related to prolonged and heavy rainfall and severe
weather that occurred across the Colorado's Front Range and the Northwest part of the
state that began in late April 2015, which has continued through May and June 2015. This
severe weather resulted in persistent flooding, tornadoes, sinkholes, subsidence, erosion,
landslides, debris flows, and agricultural impacts to include crop and livestock loss.
Consequently, the counties of Baca, Elbert, El Paso, Fremont, Logan, Morgan, Pueblo,
Saguache, Sedgwick, Washington, and Yuma have all declared disasters, highlighting the
gravity of the continuous severe weather pattern.
1.
Background and Purpose
The Governor is responsible for meeting the dangers to the state and people
presented by disasters. The Colorado Disaster Emergency Act defines a disaster as "the
occurrence or imminent threat of widespread or severe damages, injury or loss of life
or property resulting from any natural cause or cause of human origin, including but not
limited to fire, flood, earthquake, wind, storm ...." C.R.S. § 24-33.5-703(3).
Beginning in mid-April 2015, a destructive weather pattern impacted Colorado and
has persisted through May and June 2015. Damage to public infrastructure began on April
28, 2015, and homes were lost to tornadoes on June 4, 2015. Record amounts of rainfall
fell across Colorado, with widespread impacts being felt across many counties and
municipalities. Some areas of the Eastern Plains experienced between 200% and 600%
above average rainfall.
---PAGE---
Executive Order D 2015-005
July 2, 2015
Page 2 of 4
In many locations, excessive rainfall exceeded both daily and monthly precipitation
records. This prolonged weather pattern triggered destructive effects in the affected counties
including loss of structures, sinkholes, subsidence, erosion, landslides, debris flows,
recurring flooding within various river basins and streams, all of which resulted in
widespread damage to property, infrastructure, and agriculture. Collectively, these
damages imposed significant and costly burdens to affected communities requiring state-
level assistance for response and recovery activities. Furthermore, state efforts are
needed to mitigate current and future threats to persons and property. Additional
municipalities and counties-beyond those that have already declared an emergencies-
continue to assess their damages and costs. Due to the excessive precipation, slope failures
and slope instabilities may occur in the coming weeks even after the rains have subsided.
Related to the weather conditions landslides have occurred across the state, particularly
in Northwest Colorado. For example, both the northbound and southbound lanes of State
Highway 13 ('SH 13") have experienced major damage. The extent of the damage to SH 13 and
other highways in the state requires immediate action.
Declaration and Directives
A. The severe weather resulting in the occurrence of persistent flooding, tornadoes,
sinkholes, subsidence, erosion, landslides, debris flows, and associated agricultural
impacts and infrastructure damage constitutes a disaster emergency under C.R.S.
§ 24-33.5-701, et. seq. The Governor's verbal order of May 9, 2015, declaring a dister
emergency is hereby memorialized by this Executive Order and shall have the full force
and effect of law as if it were contained within this Executive Order. Further, the threat
of danger has not passed, and therefore, the initial declaration of a disaster is renewed
for an additional thirty days from June 9, 2015.
B. This order applies to the impacted communities east of the Continental Divide bounded

of life, destruction of hundreds of residential and other structures, damage to businesses,

all 39 counties in the state. Given the gravity of the situation, the State of Washington has
requested Colorado National Guard resources to assist with the firefighting effort in
accordance with the EMAC. Under the EMAC, Colorado National Guard resources may
supplement local response efforts to preserve life and property and to meet the
emergency needs of the State of Washington. Pursuant to C.R.S. § 28-3-104 and the EMAC,

request on Friday, August 21, 2015. This Executive Order memorializes my verbal order.

portions of the Colorado Disaster Emergency Act, C.R.S. § 24-33.5-701, et seq. I,

1. Background and Purpose
During the early morning hours of March 23, 2016, blizzard conditions began
forming in northeast Colorado, including the Denver metropolitan area. Emergency
personnel anticipated that the rapid accumulation of snow and high winds had the
potential to strand motorists throughout the area, thereby necessitating rescue
missions. It was likely that the demand for rescue missions would exceed the
capacity of local agencies. Accordingly, pursuant to C.R.S. § 28-3-104, Governor
Hickenlooper verbally authorized the activation of the National Guard to assist these
rescue missions.
As the day progressed, the blizzard intensified, resulting in closures of
numerous highways along the Front Range from the Wyoming border to Colorado
Springs and throughout Northeastern Colorado. Denver International Airport shut
down at approximately 12:17 p.m. as blizzard conditions triggered power
fluctuations and required intensive snow removal. At approximately 3:40 p.m. on
March 23, 2016, Governor Hickenlooper verbally declared a disaster emergency.

Declaring a Disaster Emergency due to the Cold Springs Fire in Boulder County and Deploying the

Pursuant to the authority vested in the Governor of the State of Colorado and, in
particular, pursuant to relevant portions of C.R.S. § 28-3-104, relevant portions of the
Colorado Disaster Emergency Act, C.R.S. § 24-33.5-701, et seq., and to relevant portions
of Article IV Section 2 of the Colorado Constitution, I, Donna Lynne, Lieutenant Governor
of the State of Colorado, hereby issue this Executive Order declaring a state of disaster
emergency due to the Cold Springs Fire in Boulder County and deploying the National
Guard to support emergency response and fire suppression operations.
1.
Background and Purpose
On Saturday, July 9, 2016, an improperly extinguished campfire ignited a fire near
Nederland in Boulder County. The fire was named the Cold Springs Fire, and the initial
fire management objectives were to confine and contain the fire. Due to the extreme
conditions, potential for fire growth, and lives and property at risk, the Colorado Division of
Homeland Security and Emergency Management proactively requested activation of the
State Emergency Operations Plan and pre-authorization for use of the Colorado National
Guard if requests for assistance and resources were received from Boulder County. As acting
Governor at the time because Governor Hickenlooper was traveling out of state, I verbally
approved the request on July 9, 2016 at approximately 3:30 p.m.
Late in the afternoon on July 9, 2016, Boulder County declared a local emergency due
to limited resources, size of the fire, and lives and property at risk. The Division of Fire
Prevention and Control declared the fire eligible for funding from the Emergency Fire Fund
at 5:20 p.m. on July 9, 2016.
---PAGE---
Executive Order D 2016-004
July 15 2016
Page 2 of 3
Late in the evening on July 9, 2016, Boulder County made an official request to
the Colorado Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management for use of the
Colorado National Guard. The National Guard assets began assisting at 7:00 a.m. on July
10, 2016.
At approximately 6:30 p.m. on July 10, 2016 the Federal Emergency Management
Agency determined that the Cold Springs Fire qualified as a Fire Management Assistance
Grant emergency. As of the morning of July 11, the Cold Springs Fire had burned 606 acres
and was two miles northeast of Nederland in Boulder County. Containment was at zero
percent. More than 1,900 people were evacuated, and five homes and other structures
were destroyed.
Il.
Declaration and Directives
A. This fire constitutes a disaster emergency under C.R.S. § 24-33.5-704. My verbal
order of July 9, 2016 declaring a disaster emergency and authorizing the use of the
Colorado National Guard for up to 30 days pursuant to C.R.S. § 28-3-104 is hereby
memorialized by this Executive Order and shall have the full force and effect of law
as if it were contained within this Executive Order.
B. The State Emergency Operations Plan is hereby activated. All State departments
and agencies shall take whatever actions may be required and requested by the
Director or Acting Director of the Office of Emergency Management, including the
provision of appropriate staff and equipment as necessary.
C. Pursuant to C.R.S. § 24-33.5-706(4), $7,000,000 in the Disaster Emergency Fund is
encumbered to pay for response and recovery efforts related to the Cold Spring Fire.
These funds are eligible for use immediately upon exhaustion of the Emergency
Fire Fund. The Emergency Management Director is hereby authorized and directed
to allocate these funds to the appropriate government agencies and to execute
awards, purchase orders, or other mechanisms to effect the allocation of these
funds. These funds shall remain available for this purpose for thirty-six months
from July 9, 2016, and any unexpended funds shall remain in the Disaster
Emergency Fund.
HI.
Duration
This Executive Order shall expire thirty days from July 9, 2016, unless extended
further by Executive Order, except that the funds described in paragraph I|(C) above
shall remain available for the described purposes for thirty-six months from July 9, 2016.

for the Historic Flooding of September 2013
Pursuant to the authority vested in the Governor of the State of Colorado and, in
particular, pursuant to relevant portions of C.R.S. § 28-3-104 and relevant portions of the
Colorado Disaster Emergency Act, C.R.S. § 24-33.5-701, et seq., I, John W. Hickenlooper,
Governor of the State of Colorado, hereby issue this Executive Order amending
Executive Order D 2014-012 to extend the availability of funds for recovery from the
historic flooding of September 2013.
Background and Purpose
The Governor is responsible for meeting the dangers to the state and people
presented by disasters. C.R.S. 924-33.5-704. The Colorado Disaster Emergency Act defines a
disaster as "the occurrence or imminent threat of widespread or severe damages, injury or
loss of life or property resulting from any natural cause or cause of human origin, including
but not limited to fire, flood, earthquake, wind, storm...." C.R.S. §24-33.5-703(3).
In the wake of the historic flooding in September 2013, I issued executive orders to
address the enormous challenges faced by the people of Colorado. Due to the great
destructive nature of the flooding and the multitude of complexities associated with the
reconstruction projects, many projects have not yet reached full completion. Local
governments continue to work diligently to complete recovery projects and it is projected
that these complicated projects will reach closeout on or before December 2021.
This Executive Order extends the availability of Disaster Emergency Funds to
continue to support critical, ongoing recovery efforts.

Amendment

Duration

EXECUTIVE ORDER
Declaring a Disaster Emergency due to the Hayden Pass Fire in
Fremont County and Deploying the National Guard to Assist with Response
Pursuant to the authority vested in the Governor of the State of Colorado and, in
particular, pursuant to relevant portions of C.R.S. § 28-3-104, relevant portions of the
Colorado Disaster Emergency Act, C.R.S. 9 24-33.5-701, et seq., and to relevant portions
of Article IV Section 2 of the Colorado Constitution, I, John W. Hickenlooper, Governor of
the State of Colorado, hereby issue this Executive Order declaring a disaster emergency
due to the Hayden Pass Fire in Fremont County and deploying the National Guard to
support emergency response and fire suppression operations.
Background and Purpose
On Friday, July 8, 2016 at 6:00 p.m., lightning ignited a fire in the San Isabel National
Forest. On Sunday, July 10, 2016, the fire increased in size and moved toward Coaldale in
Fremont County. The fire was named the Hayden Pass Fire, and the initial fire
management objectives were to confine and contain the fire. Due to the extreme
conditions, potential for fire growth, lives and property at risk, and requests for state
assistance with fire suppression and traffic control points, the Colorado Division of
Homeland Security and Emergency Management proactively requested activation of the
State Emergency Operations Plan and pre-authorization for use of the Colorado National
Guard in the event that Fremont County made requests for assistance and resources.
Lieutenant Governor Donna Lynne, who was acting as Governor as I was out of state,
verbally approved the request on July 12, 2016 at approximately 10:30 a.m.
On July 12, 2016, Fremont County declared a local emergency due to limited
resources, size of the fire, and lives and property at risk. The Division of Fire Prevention
and Control declared the fire eligible for funding from the Emergency Fire Fund on July 11,
2016.
---PAGE---
Executive Order D 2016-006
July 20 2016
Page 2 of 3
As of the morning of July 14, the Hayden Pass Fire had burned over 12,000 acres and
was threatening the town of Coaldale in Fremont County. Containment was at zero
percent. More than 100 homes were placed under mandatory evacuation. More than 180
campers at a youth camp sought shelter at a local high school. A Type Il federal incident
management team has taken charge of the fire on behalf of the county.
Declaration and Directives
A. This fire constitutes a disaster emergency under C.R.S. § 24-33.5-704. The Lieutenant
Governor's verbal order of July 12, 2016, declaring a disaster emergency and
authorizing the use of the Colorado National Guard for up to 30 days pursuant to
C.R.S. § 28-3-104 is hereby memorialized by this Executive Order and shall have the
full force and effect of law as if it were contained within this Executive Order.
B. The State Emergency Operations Plan is hereby activated. All State departments and
agencies shall take whatever actions may be required and requested by the Director
or Acting Director of the Office of Emergency Management, including provision of
appropriate staff and equipment as necessary.
C. Due to the current insufficiency of funds necessary to pay for fire suppression efforts
related to the Hayden Pass Fire in the Disaster Emergency Fund, I order the transfer
of $8,000,000 from the Controlled Maintenance Trust Fund into the Disaster
Emergency Fund pursuant to C.R.S. § 24-33.5-706(4)(b). I further encumber
$8,000,000 in the Disaster Emergency Fund to pay for the fire suppression, response,
and recovery efforts related to the Hayden Pass Fire since its inception. I authorize
and direct the Emergency Management Director to allocate these funds to the
appropriate government agencies and to execute awards, purchase orders, or other
mechanisms to effect the allocation of these funds. These funds shall remain
available for this purpose for thirty-six months from July 12, 2016, and any
unexpended funds shall remain in the Disaster Emergency Fund.
Duration
This Executive Order shall expire thirty days from July 12, 2016, unless extended
further by Executive Order, except that the funds described in paragraph I|(C) above
shall remain available for the described purposes for thirty-six months from July 12, 2016.

Pursuant to the authority vested in the Governor of the State of Colorado
and, in particular, pursuant to relevant portions of C.R.S. § 28-3-104, relevant

Section 2 of the Colorado Constitution, I, John W. Hickenlooper, Governor of the
State of Colorado, hereby issue this Executive Order declaring a disaster emergency
due to the Beulah Hill Fire in Pueblo County, authorizing state funding for response
to the fire and recovery from its impacts, and providing access to the State
Individual Family Grant Program.
Background and Purpose
The afternoon of Monday, October 3, 2016 a fire ignited near the Town of
Beulah in Pueblo County. The fire was named the Beulah Hill Fire. The fire spread
rapidly, placing lives and property at risk, and exceeding Pueblo County's fire
suppression capabilities. In response, Pueblo County declared a local emergency.
Because it seemed likely the fire would continue to grow, on October 3, 2016
at approximately 2:00 PM, the Colorado Division of Homeland Security and
Emergency Management proactively authorized implementation of the All-Hazards
Resource Mobilization System, pursuant to C.R.S. § 24-33.5-705.4. In the early
morning hours of October 4, 2015, the Division of Fire Prevention and Control
declared the fire eligible for funding from the Emergency Fire Fund, pursuant to
C.R.S. § 24-33.5-1220. Later in the day, the Federal Emergency Management Agency
declared the fire eligible for the Fire Management Assistance Grant Program,
pursuant to 42 U.S.C. § 5187.
---PAGE---
As predicted, the fire continued to grow, putting lives and property at risk.
The Colorado Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management
determined that the Emergency Fire Fund had been depleted earlier in 2016 due to
other fire fighting operations. Accordingly, the Division requested activation of the
State Emergency Operations Plan. I verbally approved the request on October 4,
2016 at approximately 10:00 AM.
As of the afternoon of October 4, 2016, the Beulah Hill Fire had burned over
4,800 acres and continued to threaten the Town of Beulah in Pueblo County.
Containment was at zero (0) percent. More than 779 homes were placed under
mandatory evacuation, displacing more than 1,900 residents. Several structures,
including eight homes were destroyed in the initial hours of the fire.
Il.
Declaration and Directives
This fire constitutes a disaster emergency under C.R.S. § 24-33.5-704.
My verbal order of October 4, 2016, declaring a disaster emergency
is hereby memorialized by this Executive Order and shall have the
full force and effect of law as if it were contained herein.

The State Emergency Operations Plan is hereby activated. All State
departments and agencies shall take whatever actions may be
required and requested by the Director or Acting Director of the
Office
of Emergency Management, including provision of
appropriate staff and equipment as necessary.
C.
Pursuant to C.R.S. § 24-33.5-706(4)(b), moneys in the Disaster
Emergency Fund are hereby found insufficient to pay for fire
suppression efforts related to the Beulah Hill Fire. Therefore, it is
ordered that $4,800,000 be transferred into the Disaster Emergency
Fund from the Controlled Maintenance Trust Fund. It is further
ordered that $4,800,000 be encumbered in the Disaster Emergency
Fund to pay for the fire suppression, response, and recovery efforts
related to the Beulah Hill Fire since the inception of the fire. Of this
encumbered amount, up to $100,000 is authorized in accordance
with C.R.S. § 24-33.5-1106(2) for grants of up to $5,000 to meet
necessary, disaster-related expenses of individuals or families whose
primary residence was destroyed in the Beulah Hill Fire. Further,
pursuant to C.R.S. § 24-33.5-705.4(5), the Emergency Management
Director is hereby authorized and directed to allocate these funds to
the appropriate government agencies and to execute awards,
purchase orders, or other mechanisms to effect the allocation of
these funds. These funds shall remain available for this purpose for
---PAGE---
thirty-six months from October 4, 2016, and any unexpended funds
shall remain in the Disaster Emergency Fund.

I|(C) above shall remain available for the described purposes for thirty-six months

Pursuant to the authority vested in the Governor of the State of Colorado and, in
particular, pursuant to relevant portions of C.R.S. § 28-3-104, relevant portions of the
Colorado Disaster Emergency Act, C.R.S. § 24-33.5-701, et seq. and to relevant portions of
Article IV Section 2 of the Colorado Constitution, I, John W. Hickenlooper, Governor of the

the Junkins Fire in Custer and Pueblo Counties, authorizing use of the Colorado National
Guard for fire response, and authorizing state funding for response to the fire and recovery
from its impacts.
1.
Background and Purpose
In the early morning hours of Monday, October 17, 2016 a fire ignited in Custer
County. The fire was named the Junkins Fire, and grew to an estimated 2,500 acres within
four hours and 15,751 acres by the end of the day. Low humidity, warm temperatures and
high winds contributed to the rapid growth of the fire. Approximately 130 homes were
immediately threatened in the Rye and Westcliffe areas, and an evacuation center was
established in Westcliffe. An additional 140 homes in Beulah, Pueblo County were placed
under a pre-evacuation notice. Due to the extreme conditions marked by a Red Flag
Warning issued by the National Weather Service, the fire rapidly spread throughout the day,
placing lives and property at risk. The fire exceeded Custer County's fire suppression
capabilities and the County declared a local emergency at approximately 10:00 a.m. on
October 17, 2016.
Due to the potential for further fire growth and lives and property at risk, the
Colorado Department of Public Safety proactively authorized implementation of the All-
Hazards Resource Mobilization System, pursuant to C.R.S. § 24-33.5-705.4, on October 17,
2016 at approximately 8:25 a.m. The Division of Fire Prevention determined that the Junkins
Fire was eligible for the Emergency Fire Fund, but due to previous fires, the Emergency Fire
Fund did not have funds available for the Junkins Fire.
---PAGE---
Due to continued fire growth, lives and property at risk, extent of losses, projected
recovery needs and exhaustion of the Emergency Fire Fund, the Colorado Division of
Homeland Security and Emergency Management proactively requested activation of the
State Emergency Operations Plan and authorization to utilize the National Guard. I verbally
approved the request on October 17, 2016 at approximately 9:00 a.m.
On October 18, 2016 at 9:45 p.m., FEMA Region VIll Acting Regional Administrator
Nancy Dragani approved the Division of Fire Prevention and Control's request for a federal
Fire Management Assistance Grant.
Il.
Declaration and Directives
A. This fire constitutes a disaster emergency under C.R.S. § 24-33.5-704. My
verbal order of October 17, 2016, declaring a disaster emergency and
authorizing use of the National Guard is hereby memorialized by this Executive
Order and shall have the full force and effect of law as if it were contained
within this Executive Order.
B. The State Emergency Operations Plan is hereby activated. All State
departments and agencies shall take whatever actions may be required and
requested by the Director or Acting Director of the Office of Emergency
Management, including provision of appropriate staff and equipment as
necessary.
Pursuant to C.R.S. § 24-33.5-706(4)(b), moneys in the Disaster Emergency Fund are
hereby found insufficient to pay for fire suppression efforts related to the Junkins
Fire. I therefore transfer $7,000,000 into the Disaster Emergency Fund from the
Controlled Maintenance Trust Fund. I further encumber $7,000,000 in the Disaster
Emergency Fund to pay for the fire suppression, response, and recovery efforts
related to the Junkins Fire since the inception of the fire. Pursuant to C.R.S. § 24-
33.5-705.4(5), I hereby authorize and direct the Emergency Management Director
to allocate these funds to the appropriate government agencies and to execute
awards, purchase orders, or other mechanisms to effect the allocation of these
funds. These funds shall remain available for this purpose for thirty-six months
from October 17, 2016, and any unexpended funds shall remain in the Disaster
Emergency Fund.
---PAGE---
III.
Duration
This Executive Order shall expire thirty days from October 17, 2016, unless extended
further by Executive Order, except that the funds described in paragraph I|(C) above
shall remain available for the described purposes for thirty-six months from October 17,
2016.

in the early afternoon hours of Sunday, September 4, 2016, a fire ignited in Larimer

pursuant to relevant portions of the Colorado Disaster Emergency Act, C.R.S. § 24-33.5-701, et seq.,
I, Governor John W. Hickenlooper, Governor of the State of Colorado, hereby issue this Executive
Order extending the availability of funds and providing additional funds to pay for costs associated
with the disaster emergency due to the 2012 Cedar Knob Fire.
Background and Purpose
The Governor is responsible for meeting the dangers to the state and people presented by
disasters. The Colorado Disaster Emergency Act defines a disaster as "the occurrence or imminent
threat of widespread or severe damage, injury, or loss of life or property resulting from any natural
cause or cause of human origin, including but not limited to fire ...." C.R.S. § 24-33.5-703(3).
In July 2012, Moffat County had multiple fire starts, which came to be known as the Cedar
Knob Fire and related Moffat County Fires. Moffat County requested State assistance to help with
fire suppression, response, and recovery efforts related to the Cedar Knob fire and other wildfires in
Moffat County. Moffat County worked with the Bureau of Land Management to utilize federal
resources to assist.
This Office declared a disaster emergency due to the Cedar Knob Fire in Executive Order D
2012-051. In that Executive Order, I encumbered $110,000 in the Disaster Emergency Fund for fire
suppression, response, and recovery efforts in connection with the Cedar Knob Fire and related
Moffat County Fires. Pursuant to Executive Order D 2012-051, the funds were available until
January 2014.
As recovery efforts progressed, the Colorado Department of Public Safety determined that it
required additional time and resources to address sufficiently the impacts of the Cedar Knob Fire
and related Moffat County Fires. Accordingly, the Department of Public Safety has requested an
additional $1,851 to assist with the recovery efforts and requested that funds be available through

and the Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management are authorized

appropriate and permitted by law.

Pursuant to the authority vested in the Governor of the State of Colorado and, in particular,
pursuant to relevant portions of the Colorado Disaster Emergency Act, C.R.S. § 24-33.5-701, et seq.,
I, Governor John W. Hickenlooper, Governor of the State of Colorado, hereby issue this Executive
Order extending the availability of funds and providing additional funds to pay for costs associated
with the disaster emergency due to the June 2012 Pine Ridge Fire.
1.
Background and Purpose
The Governor is responsible for meeting the dangers to the state and people presented by
disasters. The Colorado Disaster Emergency Act defines a disaster as "the occurrence or imminent
threat of widespread or severe damage, injury, or loss of life or property resulting from any natural
cause or cause of human origin, including but not limited to fire ...." C.R.S. § 24-33.5-703(3).
In June 2012, a wildfire named the Pine Ridge Fire started in Mesa County on lands
managed by the Bureau of Land Management. The fire grew rapidly being fueled by extremely dry

Background and Purpose
The Governor is responsible for meeting the dangers to the state and people presented by
disasters. The Colorado Disaster Emergency Act defines a disaster as "the occurrence or imminent
threat of widespread or severe damage, injury, or loss of life or property resulting from any natural
cause or cause of human origin, including but not limited to wildfire C.R.S § 24-33.5-703(3).
Mid-day March 6, 2017, a fire was reported in Logan County. At the time, most of eastern
Colorado was under a red flag warning due to high fire danger. A high wind warning was also in
effect, with wind gusts around 50 miles per hour. These conditions allowed the fire to grow and
spread rapidly, and local capabilities were quickly overwhelmed. Schools and homes were ordered
to evacuate. The fire spread east to neighboring Phillips County. Fires were also reported in other
Colorado Counties, as well as western Kansas. By early evening, four structures, including three
homes, as well as 30,000 acres, had burned. The State Emergency Operations Center activated to
fulfill requests for an Incident Management Team, fire engines, and caches of radios. Logan County
verbally declared a local emergency March 6, 2017, and ratified the decision in writing March 7,
2017.
At approximately 9:00 p.m. on March 6, 2017, I verbally declared a disaster emergency for
wildfire in Logan and Phillips Counties and activated the State of Colorado Hazard and Incident
Response and Recovery Plan, also known as the State Emergency Operations Plan.

from any natural cause or cause of human origin, including but not limited to fire ...." C.R.S §

The Peekaboo fire is believed to have been caused by a lightning strike on June 27,
2017. It is burning on federal land in pinyon-juniper, grass and sagebrush fuels. The fire
threatened multiple ranches, Dinosaur National Monument, and Browns Park National Wildlife
refuge. The area affected by the fire is also prime sage grouse habitat.

Due to persistent hot, dry conditions, the fire grew rapidly on July 6, more than doubling
in size in one day. Federal land managers initially allowed the fire to burn for the environmental
benefit of natural fire, but the rapid growth, properties at risk, and the need to protect habitat
for the endangered sage grouse led federal land managers to pursue full suppression of the fire.

declared a disaster emergency for the Peekaboo Fire and activated the State of Colorado
Hazard and Incident Response and Recovery Plan, also known as the State Emergency

of the standby aircraft and personnel will be reimbursed to Colorado by the United States
Forest Service.
Background and Purpose
The Governor is responsible for meeting the dangers to the state and people presented
by disasters. The Colorado Disaster Emergency Act defines a disaster as "the occurrence or
imminent threat of widespread or severe damage, injury, or loss of life or property resulting
from any natural cause or cause of human origin, including but not limited to fire ...." C.R.S §
24-33.5-703(3).
Beginning in June 2017, dry and hot conditions increased the wildland fire risk across
Colorado. Numerous wildland fires in Colorado and surrounding states in June and July reduced
the availability of aircrafts customarily used for initial suppression of new wildland fire starts in
Colorado. A strong, timely initial response is proven to substantially reduce the risk to life and

July 19, 2017
Page 2 of 3
property and lower the cost of fighting fires. The Colorado National Guard can provide aircraft
to support initial suppression of wildland fire.
At approximately 3:00 pm on July 7, 2017, Governor Hickenlooper verbally declared a
disaster emergency due to wildland fire in Colorado and activated the State of Colorado Hazard
and Incident Response and Recovery Plan, also known as the State Emergency Operations Plan.
He further verbally authorized deployment and use of the Colorado National Guard to
provide standby aircraft and personnel to support the initial suppression of wildland fire in
Colorado.

C.R.S 9 24-33.5-701, et seq. Governor Hickenlooper's verbal order of July 7, 2017
declaring a disaster emergency is hereby memorialized by this Executive Order and
shall have the full force and effect of law as if it were contained within this order.
B. Pursuant to 42 U.S.C. § 1856a and the Colorado Statewide Cooperative Wildland Fire
Management and Stafford Act Response Agreement, the United States Forest Service
Rocky Mountain Region will reimburse costs the Colorado National Guard incurs from
this aircraft and personnel standby service. To assure timely reimbursement to the
Colorado National Guard, 1 authorize payment from the Wildfire Cost Recovery Fund,
managed by the Division of Fire Prevention and Control, to pay for costs associated
with the aircraft and personnel standby service. Costs shall be assigned to each
incident as it occurs, and shall be reimbursed according to the processes and funding
sources determined for each incident.
C. I authorize and direct the Division of Fire Prevention and Control to coordinate
application to the federal government for funds available for reimbursement,
including funds expended as authorized in Paragraph IIB. The Division shall use funds
from such federal reimbursements to reimburse the State for expending funds in the
Wildfire Cost Recovery Fund to reimburse the Colorado National Guard.
D. Governor Hickenlooper's verbal orders of July 7, 2017 activating and authorizing the
use of the National Guard assets for wildland fire initial suppression missions are
hereby memorialized by this Executive Order and shall have the full force and effect of
law as if they were contained within this order.

EXECUTIVE ORDER

impacts and events relating to the 2017 Solar Eclipse
Pursuant to the authority vested in the Governor of the State of Colorado and, in
particular, pursuant to the Colorado Constitution, Article TV, Section 2, and pursuant to the
relevant portions of the Colorado Disaster Emergency Act, C.R.S § 24-33.5-701, et seq., I, John
W. Hickenlooper, Governor of the State of Colorado, hereby issue this Executive Order
declaring a state of disaster emergency due to the anticipated impacts and events in Colorado
related to the 2017 Solar Eclipse in northern Colorado. Further, pursuant to the Colorado
Constitution, Article IV, Section 5, and pursuant to C.R.S. § 28-3-104, I also hereby authorize
Colorado National Guard air resources to respond to impacts and events relating to the 2017
Solar Eclipse in northern Colorado.
I.
Background and Purpose
The Governor is responsible for meeting the dangers to the state and people presented by
disasters. The Colorado Disaster Emergency Act defines a disaster as "the occurrence or
imminent threat of widespread or severe damage, injury, or loss of life or property resulting from
any natural cause or cause of human origin ...." C.R.S § 24-33.5-703(3).
On Monday, August 21, 2017, a solar eclipse occurred with the path of totality crossing
the nation from west to east, including portions of Wyoming and Nebraska. The event attracted
interest across the nation, with an estimated 200 million people living within a one-day drive of
the path of totality. A substantial number of people from Colorado made the journey to
neighboring states, leading to traffic congestion, vehicle crashes, additional need for law
enforcement and emergency medical services personnel and other associated impacts.
---PAGE---
Executive Order D 2017-020
September 11, 2017
Page 2 of 3
In the week prior to the 2017 Solar Eclipse, the Colorado Department of Transportation
as well as other experts in the transportation arena predicted that the eclipse traffic could be the
most significant traffic event of the year. There was significant concern that this would be a
major traffic event - both from the heavy traffic volume as well as disruptions due to the eclipse.
Experts predicted that up to 600,000 additional people would travel to Wyoming to view the
eclipse. The Department of Transportation predicted that up to 400,000 additional people could
be on Colorado roadways over the weekend and Monday August 21st. On August 18, 2017, the
Colorado Department of Transportation warned drivers to be ready for an 8-12 hour wait to
return home after the eclipse. In addition, the State Emergency Operations Center expected the
traffic to overwhelm the response capabilities of local governments and private sector entities.
Due to the information and projections of significant traffic and delays leaving motorists
on our highways for 8-12 hours and in anticipation of the potential impacts resulting from this,
on August 18, 2017, I verbally declared a disaster emergency for responding to impacts related
to the 2017 Solar Eclipse, and activated the State of Colorado Hazard and Incident Response and
Recovery Plan, also known as the State Emergency Operations Plan. The State Emergency
Operations Center began final preparations August 18, 2017 to support local and state agency
emergency needs, and activated them August 20-21, 2017 to closely monitor conditions and
provide for rapid response to local and state agency assistance requests. Of particular concern
were anticipated requests for emergency medical evacuation of sick and injured patients that
would require helicopter evacuation due to congested roadways in remote areas.
Further, I authorized pre-positioning of Colorado National Guard air resources for
impacts and events related to the 2017 Solar Eclipse in northern Colorado, including helicopter
medical emergency transportation and wildland fire suppression. Colorado National Guard air
resources were placed on standby beginning August 21, 2017, at 10:00 a.m. and continued until
5:00 p.m., and the State Emergency Operations Center provided staff to allow state agencies to
organize responsive activities. The State provided direct assistance to local law enforcement
through the Colorado State Patrol, the State Emergency Operations Center, and the Department
of Transportation. The National Guard remained on standby, but their assistance was not
ultimately necessary.
II.
Declarations and Directives
A. The 2017 Solar Eclipse and associated impacts constitute a disaster emergency under
C.R.S § 24-33.5-701, et seq. My verbal order of August 18, 2017 declaring a disaster
emergency to prepare for and respond to impacts of the 2017 Solar Eclipse is hereby
memorialized by this Executive Order and shall have the full force and effect of law
as if it were contained within this order.
---PAGE---
Executive Order D 2017-020
September 11, 2017
Page 3 of 3
B. The State of Colorado Hazard and Incident Response and Recovery Plan, also known
as the State Emergency Operations Plan, is hereby activated. All State departments
and agencies shall take whatever actions may be required and requested by the
Director or Acting Director of the Office of Emergency Management pursuant to the
Emergency Support Function 5 Annex of the Colorado Hazard and Incident Response
and Recovery Plan, including provision of appropriate staff and equipment as
necessary.
C. Due to the current insufficiency of funds necessary to pay for responding to impacts
related to the 2017 Solar Eclipse in the Disaster Emergency Fund, I order the transfer
of S30,000 from the Controlled Maintenance Trust Fund into the Disaster Emergency
Fund pursuant to C.R.S. § 24-33.5-706(4)(b). I further encumber $30,000 in the
Disaster Emergency Fund to pay for responding to the impacts related to the 2017
Solar Eclipse, including preparations and activating the State Emergency Operations
Center since August 18, 2017, and placing Colorado National Guard personnel on
standby August 21, 2017.
D. My verbal orders of August 18, 2017, activating the Colorado National Guard and
authorizing the use of Colorado National Guard aviation assets for 2017 Solar Eclipse
missions are hereby memorialized by this Executive Order and shall have the full
force and effect of law as if they were contained within this order.
II. Duration
This Executive Order shall expire thirty days from August 18, 2017, unless extended
further by Executive Order, except that the funds described in paragraph IIc) above shall remain
available for the described purposes for sixty (60) months from the date of this Executive Order.

The Governor is responsible for meeting the dangers to the state and people presented by
disasters. The Colorado Disaster Emergency Act defines a disaster as "the occurrence or
imminent threat of widespread or severe damage, injury, or loss of life or property resulting from
any natural cause or cause of human origin, including but not limited to ... fire" C.R.S § 24-
33.5-703(3).
Late in the morning of September 4, 2017, a fire was reported in Routt County, eight
miles northwest of Hayden. The fire was named the Deep Creek Fire. A pre-evacuation notice
was issued to residents of the Deep Creek Community, but fire crews were able to construct a
line that prevented the fire from entering the community. As of September 8, 2017, the fire grew
to 3,800 acres. The fire impacted a mix of private land and land under the control of the federal
Bureau of Land Management and thrcatened habitat of the endangered Greater Sage Grouse.
At approximately 5:45 pm on September 8, 2017, Governor Hickenlooper verbally
declared a disaster emergency for wildland fire in Routt County.

Las Vegas, Nevada was recently the site of the worst mass shooting in modern United
States history. The gunman opened fire on a crowd of concert attendees, killing at least 58 people
and injuring nearly 500. The number of fatalities and complexities of the investigation exceeded
local capabilities.
As a party to the Emergency Management Assistance Compact, C.R.S. § 24-60-2901 et
seq., the State of Colorado is able to provide assistance to states and certain United States
Territories enduring a disaster emergency. The State of Nevada, also a party to the Compact,
requested that Denver County's Director of the Office of the Medical Examiner travel to Las
Vegas to provide technical assistance to Nevada's Clark County Medical Examiner.
By this Order, I authorize personnel from Colorado to respond to Nevada's request for
assistance.

related to the Las Vegas Mass Shooting.
B. Pursuant to C.R.S. § 24-60-2901 et seq., I hereby implement the Emergency Management
Assistance Compact. The State of Colorado shall provide personnel to assist Nevada in
emergency response efforts related to the Las Vegas Mass Shooting.

management to encumber $5,000 from the Resource Mobilization Fund, pursuant to

Background and Purposc
The Governor is responsible for meeting the dangers to the State and people presented by
disasters. C.R.S. § 24-33.5-704(1). The Colorado Disaster Emergency Act defines a disaster as
"the occurrence or imminent threat of widespread or severe damagc, injury, or loss of life or
property resulting from any natural cause or cause of human origin, including but not limited to
fire." C.R.S. § 24-33.5-703(3).
In July 2012, two wildfires, the Powell Fire and the Little Duck Fire (the "Powell
Complex"), started in Rio Blanco County on lands managed by the Bureau of Land
Management. The fires grew rapidly due lo extremely dry vegetation, low relative humidity,
high temperatures, and windy conditions. Lightning strikes are believed to have caused both
fires. On July 21, 2012, the Colorado Division of Fire Prevention and Control received a request
from the Rio Blanco County Sheriff to assume charge of the Powell Complex in accord with the
Emergency Fire Fund Agreement. The State accepted the Powell Complex as an Emergency
Fire Fund-designated fire. By July 24, 2012, the fires had spread to approximately 1,650 acres.

July 16, 2018
Page 2 of 3
In Executive Order D 2012 034, 1 memorialized a verbal declaration of a state of disaster
emergency due to the Powell Complex and ordered the transfer of two hundred ten thousand
dollars ($210,000) from the Control Maintenance Trust Fund to the Disaster Emergency Fund for
fire suppression efforts in connection with the Powell Complex. Pursuant to Executive Order D
2012 034, those funds were available through July 24, 2013.
The 2011 and 2012 wildfire scasons resulted in a record-breaking number of fatalities
and extraordinary damage to homes, forest lands, and agricultural assets. As a result, in
Executive Order D 2013 014, I extended the availability of funds for the Powell Complex and a
number of other fire-related disaster emergencies until January 31, 2014.
Upon a determination by the Colorado Department of Public Safety ("CDPS") that it
required additional time and resources to sufficiently address the impacts of the Powell Complex,
I issued Executive Order D 2017 004 to extend the availability of existing funds until
December 3l, 2016, and to encumber an additional one hundred six thousand, seventy-eight
dollars ($106,078) in the Disaster Emergency Fund.
As recovery efforts conclude, CDPS has determined that it requires additional time to
finalize expenses for some older wildfires, including the Powell Complex. Further, CDPS
requires three thousand one hundred thirty-eight dollars (S3,138) to reimburse the Bureau of
Indian Affairs for costs incurred during firefighting and recovery efforts relating to the Powell
Complex. This Executive Order therefore extends the availability of the funding provided for
the Powell Complex in Executive Orders D 2017 004 and D 2012 034 until December 31, 2018,
to allow for payment of final expenses related to the wildfire. This Exccutive Order also
encumbers an additional three thousand one hundred thirty-eight dollars ($3,138) in the Disaster
Emergency Fund to pay the State's outstanding obligation to the Bureau of Indian Affairs.

Pursuant to the authority vested in the Governor of the State of Colorado and, in

Department of Public Health and Environment to extend the suspension of certain regulations
and licensing requirements in order to support responders to wildland fires.
Further, pursuant to Article IV, Section 5 of the Colorado Constitution and pursuant to
C.R.S. § 28-3-104, I hereby issue this Executive Order amending Executive Orders D 2018 006
and D 2018 018 to extend the deployment of the Colorado National Guard for the purpose of
responding to fires by providing aircraft, equipment, and personnel to support fire suppression
efforts.
I.
Background and Purpose
The Governor is responsible for meeting the dangers to the State and people presented
by disasters. C.R.S. § 24-33.5-704(I). The Colorado Disaster Emergency Act defines a disaster
as "the occurrence or imminent threat of widespread or severe damage, injury, or loss of life or
property resulting from any natural cause or cause of human origin, including but not limited to
fire." C.R.S. § 24-33.5-703(3).
Beginning in March 2018, dry and hot conditions increased the wildland fire risk across
Colorado and other western states. In June, July, August, and September 2018, numerous
---PAGE---

September 19, 2018
Page 2 of 4
wildland fires broke out throughout western and southern Colorado. State and local
communities mobilized all available equipment and personnel to conduct fire suppression and
support activities, but the need is so great that current resources are at or beyond capacity. The
Colorado National Guard can provide aircraft, equipment, and personnel ("National Guard
Assets") to support firefighting operations.
Due to the expected continuation of hot and dry weather conditions in Colorado, and
the need for additional firefighting resources, particularly helicopters that can be used for
firefighting operations, this Executive Order extends my declaration of a disaster emergency,
extends the deployment of the Colorado National Guard, and authorizes the Colorado
Department of Public Health and Environment to extend the suspension of certain regulations
and licensing requirements in order to support responders to wildland fires.
On June 16, 2018, I authorized the Colorado Department of Public Health and
Environment to suspend regulations and licensing requirements for thirty (30) days for out-of-
state paramedics and emergency medical technicians providing support to responders to
wildland fires. As wildland fires continued into July, August, and September, the reduced
availability of paramedics and emergency medical technicians continued, requiring the State to
request additional out-of-state paramedics and emergency medical technicians. Continued
suspension of regulations and licensing requirements is necessary for the safety and health of
personnel responding to wildland fires in Colorado. This Executive Order extends the Colorado
Department of Public Health and Environment's authorization to suspend regulations and
licensing requirements for an additional thirty (30) days from August 28, 2018.
Based upon an increased number of major fire incidents across Colorado, at 2:30 PM
on June 20, 2018, I verbally authorized expanding the supporting role of the Colorado National
Guard to include assistance to firefighting operations for fires where the State of Colorado has
responsibility for fire suppression pursuant to C.R.S. § 24-33.5-1221(1).
At approximately 12:10 PM on June 29, 2018, I verbally declared a disaster emergency
for wildland fire in Colorado in order to authorize deployment of the Colorado National Guard
to provide National Guard Assets to support emergency search and rescue missions associated
with fires throughout the state. I also activated the State of Colorado Hazard and Incident
Response and Recovery Plan ("State Emergency Operations Plan").

on June 30, 2018, I verbally authorized expanding the supporting role of the Colorado National

as "the occurrence or imminent threat of widespread or severe damage, injury, or loss of life or

703(3).
On April 10, 2019, meteorologists predicted that an extremely powerful spring storm
would impact Colorado, with counties north of Interstate 70 and east of Interstate 25
experiencing the greatest impact. Snow accumulation of 12 inches was expected, with wind gusts
up to 60 miles per hour that could create blowing and drifting snow, forcing closures of major
highways and cancellation of passenger flights. The National Weather Service issued a blizzard
warning for the most highly-impacted areas. Based on experience with a similar storm in March
2019, the State expected that travelers would become stranded on roadways and require
sheltering. The Colorado National Guard is the most effective available resource to support
search and rescue operations in those types of conditions.

Operations Center to support and coordinate search and rescue activities and other requests from

Colorado Hazard and Incident Response and Recovery Plan (State Emergency Operations
Plan"). At the same time, I verbally authorized deployment and use of the Colorado National
Guard for the purpose of search and rescue operations resulting from the Eastern Colorado
Counties Severe Spring Weather and Blizzard Conditions.
Declarations and Directives
A. The Eastern Colorado Counties Severe Spring Weather and Blizzard Conditions
and associated impacts constitute a disaster emergency under C.R.S § 24-33.5-
701, et seq. My verbal order of April 10, 2019, declaring a disaster emergency is
hereby memorialized by this Executive Order and shall have the full force and
effect of law as if it were contained within this Executive Order.
B.
Further, pursuant to C.R.S. § 28-3-104, my verbal orders of April 10, 2019,
authorizing deployment and use of the National Guard for search and rescue
operations associated with the Eastern Colorado Counties Severe Spring Weather
and Blizzard Conditions are hereby memorialized by this Executive Order and
shall have the full force and effect of law as if they were contained within this
Executive Order.
C. The State Emergency Operations Plan is hereby activated. All State departments
and agencies shall take whatever actions may be required and requested by the
Director or Acting Director of the Office of Emergency Management pursuant to
the Emergency Support Function 5 Annex of the State Emergency Operations
Plan, including provision of appropriate staff and equipment as necessary.
D.
Pursuant to C.R.S. § 24-33.5-706(4), I find that the funds regularly appropriated
to State and local agencies are insufficient to address this disaster emergency.
Therefore, I order that one hundred thousand dollars ($100,000) from the Disaster
Emergency Fund is encumbered to pay for the response, recovery, and mitigation
efforts related to this disaster emergency. This amount is currently available in
the Disaster Emergency Fund.
E.
Further, pursuant to C.R.S. § 24-33.5-705.4(5), the Director of the Office of
Emergency Management is hereby authorized and directed to allocate the funding
to the appropriate government agencies and non-profit organizations and execute
awards, purchase orders, or other mechanisms to effect the allocation of the funds.
These funds shall remain available for this purpose until six (6) months from the

Duration
This Executive Order shall expire thirty (30) days from April 10, 2019, unless extended
further by Executive Order, except that the funds described in Section II(D) above shall remain
available for the described purposes for six (6) months from the date of this Executive Order.
